candidates.attacker_control: The whole XML/JSON stream passed to XStreamer.fromXML(String/Reader/InputStream, ...) is attacker-controlled: (1) the first object is the embedded com.thoughtworks.xstream.XStream instance, whose private fields (mapper chain, converter lookup/registry, marshalling strategy, securityMapper) are written as XML by XStream's normal reflection converter; (2) securityMapper.permissions is a java.util.List<TypePermission> that accepts java.util.ArrayList (allowed by the default Collection hierarchy) and any TypePermission implementation, e.g. <com.thoughtworks.xstream.security.AnyTypePermission/>; (3) all payload elements after that XStream instance are then unmarshalled by the attacker-configured instance.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the outer permission set is applied only to the embedded XStream object graph and not to the payload (XStreamer.java:261-272); checked that XStream itself defines no readResolve/writeReplace that could re-apply restrictions (text search for readResolve/writeReplace in XStream.java returned nothing); checked that SecurityMapper.permissions is plain instance state (SecurityMapper.java:28,47-52) and that permission enforcement happens at mapper.realClass time (SecurityMapper.java:72-80); checked AnyTypePermission is a public, reconstructible type (AnyTypePermission.java:15-24); checked that the payload's class-resolution path does go through the mapper/SecurityMapper (HierarchicalStreams.java:26-46). Counter-argument: XStreamer's Javadoc presents it as a self-contained utility that restores the embedded XStream 'that kept any settings' (XStreamer.java:44-51,86-94), so a defensible position is that it is intended for trusted streams; the absence of any warning and the existence of the permission-parameterized overload argue that callers are expected to configure safety, which this flow defeats.
candidates.impact: Full bypass of XStream's type-permission (security) framework whenever this public API is used on untrusted data: the attacker controls which classes may be instantiated and populated, which in XStream's documented threat model leads to remote code execution via known deserialization gadget chains and to arbitrary file/network side effects. Additionally, a caller that explicitly passes a restrictive TypePermission set to fromXML(...,permissions) gets a false sense of protection, because that set is not applied to the payload.
candidates.prerequisites: The application must call a public XStreamer.fromXML(...) overload on data it does not fully trust (network payload, message queue, stored file, etc.). The attacker needs a stream containing a serialized XStream object; such a stream is trivially produced with the complementary XStreamer.toXML(attackerXStream, payload) using an XStream instance on which addPermission(AnyTypePermission.ANY) was called. Classpath-dependent gadgets are needed for command execution; arbitrary type instantiation/field injection itself is already reachable for every class on the classpath.
candidates.root_cause: XStreamer.fromXML() first unmarshals an XStream instance out of the same attacker-controlled stream, then uses that deserialized instance - including its SecurityMapper.permissions list - to unmarshal the rest of the stream. The outer permission set (XStreamer.PERMISSIONS, or the caller-supplied TypePermission... overload) only restricts the class graph of the embedded XStream object; it deliberately allows the XStream, Mapper and TypePermission hierarchies. Because type permissions are ordinary instance state of the embedded SecurityMapper, an attacker can embed an XStream configured with AnyTypePermission.ANY (or any permissive permission) and thereby replace the effective whitelist for the payload.
candidates.title: XStreamer applies attacker-supplied XStream instance (and its type permissions) to the untrusted payload, bypassing the security framework
candidates.trace: XStreamer.fromXML(driver,xml,permissions) (XStreamer.java:259) builds an outer XStream, adds only the caller/XStreamer permissions (:261-264), and reads the first object as an XStream (:266-268). Its PERMISSIONS allow the XStream hierarchy and the TypePermission hierarchy (:55-62), so the attacker's embedded XStream, its SecurityMapper and its permissions list (including AnyTypePermission) are accepted as a valid object graph. The code then calls configured.createObjectInputStream(reader) (:269) and in.readObject() (:272); that instance's mapper chain is the embedded one, so every subsequent class-name lookup goes through the attacker-supplied SecurityMapper.realClass (SecurityMapper.java:72-80) and is authorized by the attacker-supplied permission list, whose AnyTypePermission.allows() returns true for every type (AnyTypePermission.java:21-24). The caller's permission configuration therefore no longer constrains the payload. XStream's own default deny-by-default whitelist (XStream.java setupSecurity, :633-690) and any NoTypePermission/deny rules supplied by the caller are silently replaced for the payload.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no runtime confirmation was performed (per review constraints). Exploitability for code execution depends on the victim classpath containing a usable gadget chain, and on the application actually using XStreamer.fromXML for attacker-influenced data. I could not compare against upstream history/patch records (no external access), so I cannot state whether this exact bypass corresponds to a published CVE; the candidate is a source-evidenced lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data / CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization (security-framework bypass via attacker-controlled configuration)

coverage_summary: Source scope reported by get_source_scope: 477 readable files (no files excluded by size/symlink/sensitive-name filters; no binary files were skipped in the areas searched). Coverage focused on the shipped library xstream/src/java (345 files): full or targeted reads of the security framework (15 permission classes, SecurityMapper, CachingMapper), the mapper chain (DefaultMapper, DynamicProxyMapper, ClassAliasing/PackageAliasing/OuterClass/Array/Enum/ImmutableTypes/AnnotationMapper), the reflection and serialization converters (AbstractReflectionConverter, SerializableConverter, ExternalizableConverter, CustomObjectInputStream/OutputStream, reflection providers, FieldDictionary/SerializationMembers), the collection/enum/time/extended converters sampled in depth, the XStream facade (constructors, setupSecurity/setupConverters/setupAliases, allow/deny APIs, createObjectInputStream), the IO stack (Dom/Dom4J/JDom1+2/KXml2/Sjsxp/StandardStax/Stax/Wstx/Xom/Xpp drivers, pull readers, PrettyPrintWriter, Json/Jettison, binary, path tracking), persistence and core utilities, plus XStreamer. Spot-checked xstream-hibernate converters/mapper and skimmed xstream-jmh, xstream-benchmark and xstream-distribution (docs/website). No test sources exist in the snapshot, so behavior could not be cross-checked against tests. Not every one of the 477 files was read line-by-line; notably AnnotationMapper's full body, CGLIBEnhancedConverter, NamedMapConverter, NamedCollectionConverter, Subject/Font/Color/ActivationDataFlavor converters, and parts of the JSON/binary writers were only sampled.
limitations: No code execution, tests, scanners or exploit payloads were run; the finding is a source-code lead, not runtime-confirmed.

No access to VCS history, upstream diffs, advisory databases or patches, so I could not confirm whether this exact XStreamer behavior was later fixed or assigned a CVE; the snapshot's parent pom says 1.5.0-SNAPSHOT and its newest copyright years are 2017, but the precise commit/version line could not be established.

Exploitability for arbitrary code execution depends on the victim application using XStreamer.fromXML on untrusted input and on a usable gadget chain existing on its classpath; only arbitrary type instantiation/field population is guaranteed by the bypass.
The workflow's automatic source filters (none reported as excluding files) and the annotated-source text limit could not be cross-validated beyond the get_source_scope output.

I did not exhaustively read every file (e.g., full AnnotationMapper body, CGLIBEnhancedConverter, NamedMapConverter, JSON/binary writers), so an injected defect in an uninspected region cannot be excluded.

rejected_leads.lead: Denial of service via unbounded unmarshalling recursion (no depth/size limit) in TreeUnmarshaller.convert/AbstractReflectionConverter.doUnmarshal, triggerable by deeply nested attacker XML with plain new XStream().fromXML(...) (matches the later CVE-2022-40151/40152 family).
rejected_leads.reason: Mechanism is real and source-visible (recursive convert()/doUnmarshal, no depth or element-count limit anywhere), but it is resource exhaustion only; impact is lower than the permission bypass and it is absent from the default-usage path only in the sense of requiring deep input. Kept as an unconfirmed secondary lead rather than a second candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: XomDriver XXE / BEAStaxDriver parameter-entity XXE (io/xml/XomDriver.java uses new Builder() without disabling external entities; BEAStaxDriver sets IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false).
rejected_leads.reason: Documented as a known limitation in the snapshot's own FAQ (xstream-distribution/src/content/faq.html:708-731) for the non-default drivers, so it is not an unnoticed code defect in this snapshot and has no fix in the reviewed code.

rejected_leads.lead: CustomObjectInputStream.resolveClass uses Class.forName without consulting the SecurityMapper (core/util/CustomObjectInputStream.java:122-130).
rejected_leads.reason: In the emulated Java-serialization path the callbacks supply already-resolved objects (readObjectOverride/readFields/defaultReadObject are all overridden), so I could not establish a reachable attacker-controlled path that actually invokes resolveClass; likely dead code rather than a live bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: ArrayMapper/DefaultMapper load and initialize 'Xxx-array' component classes before the permission check; ArrayTypePermission allows any array (mapper/ArrayMapper.java:57-79, mapper/DefaultMapper.java:67-85, security/ArrayTypePermission.java:21-24).
rejected_leads.reason: Real side effect (Class.forName with initialize=true can run static initializers of non-whitelisted component types), but impact is limited to class initialization/existence probing, no demonstrated gadget, and the same behavior exists in upstream; too weak for the single candidate slot.

rejected_leads.lead: FilePersistenceStrategy escape/unescape hex-encoding inconsistency (persistence/FilePersistenceStrategy.java:114-124,150-161 uses Integer.toHexString without padding while unescape reads exactly two hex digits).
rejected_leads.reason: Only affects locally generated persistence keys; filenames/keys are not attacker-controlled through XML input, and no path traversal is reachable because '/' and '%' are escaped. Not demonstrably a remote vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Default permission list is broad and includes java.net.URL, java.io.File, java.lang.Class, java.lang.reflect.Member, Throwable, and all interfaces (XStream.java:633-690), which historically enabled SSRF/DNS side effects, file/class related gadgets and dynamic proxies (CVE-2020-26258 style).
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented intended default policy in this snapshot (xstream-distribution/src/content/security.html:139-237); I could not trace a concrete in-repo sink proving exploitability beyond what the maintainers already document as design trade-offs, so it is reported only as context, not as the candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: JavaBeanConverter invokes bean setters from attacker-controlled element/property names.
rejected_leads.reason: JavaBeanConverter is not registered by default (XStream.java:841-972); applications must opt in, so it is not a default-configuration issue in this snapshot.

summary: This is the XStream XML/Java serialization library (parent version 1.5.0-SNAPSHOT; sources' newest copyright year is 2017; no test tree). I audited the security-critical surface of the main module: the SecurityMapper/permission framework (setupSecurity defaults, Explicit/TypeHierarchy/Wildcard/RegExp/Interface/Array/No/Any permissions, addPermission semantics), the mapper chain (CachingMapper, DefaultMapper, ClassAliasingMapper, PackageAliasingMapper, ArrayMapper, DynamicProxyMapper, AnnotationMapper), the reflection/serialization converters (AbstractReflectionConverter, SerializableConverter, ExternalizableConverter, Lambda/CGLIB, PureJava/SunUnsafe reflection providers, CustomObjectInputStream/OutputStream), the collection/enum/extended converters, the XStream facade (constructors, converter registration, createObjectInputStream, allow/deny APIs, XStreamer), the IO layer (XML drivers/readers/writers, DOM/StAX/Xpp/XOM, JSON/Jettison, binary, path tracking), persistence, and core utilities, plus spot checks of xstream-hibernate, jmh and benchmark modules. I did not find any clear-cut injected or obviously deviant code; the code matches the upstream XStream master style of that era. The single strongest source-evidenced issue is a trust-boundary failure in the public XStreamer API: the type-permission configuration that governs the payload is read from the untrusted stream itself, which allows complete bypass of the (otherwise deny-by-default) security framework and therefore attacker-controlled type instantiation (RCE-capable on typical classpaths). Lower-impact/unconfirmed leads are listed separately; no runtime confirmation was performed and the payload-side gadget availability depends on the victim classpath.
